concept.technique_name: constraint substitution on a letter-number code

examples.problem_statement: In some code, letters a, b, c, d and e represent numbers 2, 4, 5, 6 and 10. We don't know which letter represents which number. Consider the following relationships: (i) a + c = e (ii) b - d = d (iii) e + a = b. Which statement below is true? (a) b = 4, d = 2 (b) a = 4, e = 6 (c) b = 6, e = 2 (d) a = 4, c = 6

solution.operation: b - d = d \Rightarrow b = 2d, with b, d \in \{2, 4, 5, 6, 10\}
solution.description: Read relationship (ii) as saying b is twice d, then look for the only pair inside the given number set where one value is double the other: 10 and 5.

solution.operation: a + c = e over the leftover values \{2, 4, 6\}: 2 + 4 = 6
solution.description: With 10 and 5 used up, only 2, 4 and 6 remain for a, c and e, and relationship (i) fixes the sum: 2 + 4 = 6, so e must be 6 while a and c share 2 and 4 in some order.
Use relationship (iii) to break the tie left over from the previous step: 6 plus a must reach b = 10, which forces a = 4 and leaves c = 2.

solution.operation: compare a = 4, e = 6 against the four options
solution.description: Check the assignment just derived against each choice; only the option stating a = 4 and e = 6 matches it.

key_reminders: b - d = d is the same as b = 2d, so scan the value set for a double.
Each letter takes a distinct value from the list, so every value fixed removes it from the remaining choices.
Use the third relationship to settle any pair still ambiguous after the first two.
common_mistakes: Reading b - d = d as b = d and discarding relationship (ii) as useless.
Stopping at \{a, c\} = \{2, 4\} and guessing the order instead of applying e + a = b.

concept.technique_name: strengthen the argument by supplying the missing link

examples.problem_statement: In the 18th and 19th centuries, it was believed in many coastal American cities that the waterfront was an undesirable location for residential buildings. As a result, much of the waterfront in these cities was never developed aesthetically and instead was left to industry and commerce. Today, however, waterfront properties are generally seen as prestigious, as evidenced by the large sums paid for homes along the beach front. A developer who wishes to make a large profit would be wise to buy urban waterfront lots and erect residential buildings on them. Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the claim made about urban waterfront properties? (A) People today have more money, relatively speaking, to spend on real estate than they did in previous centuries. (B) Homeowners will be willing to spend large sums on residential properties in traditionally industrial or commercial districts. (C) Many urban waterfront lots are available for purchase. (D) Many coastal American cities are encouraging developers to rehabilitate the waterfront through tax incentives. (E) Properties in interior residential districts in coastal American cities are significantly more expensive than those along the waterfront.

solution.operation: isolate the conclusion and the evidence offered for it
solution.result: Conclusion: a developer would be wise to buy urban waterfront lots and build residences there. Evidence: people pay large sums for beach front homes.
solution.description: Separate the claim being argued from the support given for it, since a strengthener must reinforce the link between exactly these two, and note that the task is to strengthen.

solution.operation: test (A): buyers have more money today than in past centuries
solution.description: Greater general buying power says nothing about whether the urban waterfront in particular will earn the developer money, so it leaves the argument no stronger.

solution.operation: test (B): homeowners will pay large sums in traditionally industrial or commercial districts
solution.description: The passage already told you urban waterfronts were left to industry and commerce, so a willingness to pay well in exactly those districts supplies the missing buyer for the developer's new homes.

solution.operation: test (C): many urban waterfront lots are available for purchase
solution.description: Being able to buy the lots is not being able to sell what is built on them, so availability alone does not support the profit claim.

solution.operation: test (D): coastal cities offer tax incentives for waterfront rehabilitation
solution.description: Tax breaks cut the developer's cost but still give no reason to think anyone will buy the developed properties.

solution.operation: test (E): interior properties cost significantly more than waterfront ones
solution.description: Cheaper land to acquire does not by itself establish that a profit can be made after building, and it may even hint that waterfront homes fetch less.

key_reminders: A strengthener must connect this argument's own evidence to its own conclusion, not merely be agreeable.
The profit claim needs buyers for the finished homes, so cost-side facts do not close the gap.
Details already stated in the passage (here, that urban waterfronts were industrial) are what make the right choice relevant.
common_mistakes: Picking (D) or (E) because they make the project cheaper, while the conclusion turns on whether the homes will sell.
Treating (C) as support because it makes the plan feasible rather than profitable.

examples.problem_statement: (i) What is the chance that a leap year selected randomly will have 53 Sundays? (ii) What is the chance, if the year selected is not a leap year?

solution.result: 52 Sundays are guaranteed; a 53rd depends only on the 2 leftover days
solution.description: Split the leap year's days into whole weeks plus a remainder, because the whole weeks already contribute exactly 52 Sundays and only the leftover days can add another.

solution.operation: enumerate the 7 possible consecutive-day pairs for the 2 leftover days
solution.description: The two spare days are consecutive and can start on any weekday, giving seven equally likely pairs to serve as the sample space.

solution.operation: count the pairs containing a Sunday: \{Sun-Mon, Sat-Sun\}
solution.description: Pick out the pairs that include a Sunday from the seven listed and divide that count by the total to get the leap-year chance.

solution.operation: non-leap year = 52 weeks + 1 day; favourable outcome \{Sunday\}
solution.description: Repeat the same split for a 365-day year, where only one spare day remains, so just one of the seven weekday outcomes gives a 53rd Sunday.

key_reminders: 366 = 52 weeks + 2 days and 365 = 52 weeks + 1 day; the whole weeks always supply 52 Sundays.
The leftover days of a leap year are consecutive, so the sample space is 7 day-pairs, not 7 single days.
common_mistakes: Counting Sun-Mon and Sat-Sun as one outcome and answering 1/7 for the leap year.
Treating the two extra days as independent picks and using 7 x 7 outcomes.

concept.technique_name: LCM with a constant deficit remainder

examples.problem_statement: What is the least multiple of 7, which when divided by 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, leaves the remainders 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 respectively?

solution.result: the numbers divisible by all five divisors are 60k
solution.description: Take the LCM of the divisors so that a single expression 60k captures every number leaving remainder 0 with all of them.
Notice each required remainder falls short of its divisor by the same 1, so the number sits one below a common multiple rather than one above it.
Rewrite 60k - 1 by pulling out the largest multiple of 7 available, leaving only the small term 4k - 1 to be tested for divisibility by 7.
Try k = 1, 2, ... until 4k - 1 is a multiple of 7; k = 2 is the smallest that works, which also keeps the answer least.
Substitute the k just found back into 60k - 1 to produce the required number.

key_reminders: When each remainder is a fixed amount less than its divisor, the number is LCM x k minus that amount.
LCM(2, 3, 4, 5, 6) = 60, not the product of the divisors.
Splitting 60k - 1 as 7(8k) + (4k - 1) turns the 7-divisibility test into a check on a small term.
common_mistakes: Adding the remainders instead of spotting the constant deficit of 1 and writing 60k + 1.
Taking k = 1 and answering 59 without enforcing the multiple-of-7 condition.
